claims.claim: In a cluster randomised trial of 2152 residents in 14 US nursing homes, the Mouth Care Without a Battle programme did not significantly reduce pneumonia over two years (0.67 vs 0.72 per 1000 resident-days); pneumonia was non-significantly higher in programme homes in year two; a post hoc first-year analysis found a reduction.
claims.supporting_passage: "This pragmatic cluster randomized trial observing 2152 NH residents for up to 2 years was conducted from September 2014 to May 2017. ... The study included 14 NHs from regions of North Carolina that evidenced proportionately high rehospitalization rates for pneumonia and long-term care residents." ... "During the 2-year study period, the incidence rate of pneumonia per 1000 resident-days was 0.67 and 0.72 in the intervention and control NHs, respectively. Neither the primary (unadjusted) nor secondary (covariate-adjusted) analyses found a significant reduction in pneumonia due to Mouth Care Without a Battle during 2 years (unadjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.90; upper bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 1.24; P = .27; adjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.92; upper bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 1.27; P = .30). In the second year, the rate of pneumonia was nonsignificantly higher in intervention NHs. Adjusted post hoc analyses limited to the first year found a significant reduction in pneumonia incidence in intervention NHs (IRR, 0.69; upper bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 0.94; P = .03)." ... "The lack of significant results in the second year may be associated with sustainability. Improving mouth care in US NHs may require the presence and support of dedicated oral care aides."
claims.location: Abstract: Design, Setting and Participants; Results; Conclusions and Relevance
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 2152 residents, 14 North Carolina nursing homes with high pneumonia rehospitalisation; I: Mouth Care Without a Battle (staff training programme); C: standard mouth care; O: pneumonia incidence from medical records (primary), hospitalisation and mortality (secondary); T: up to 2 years
claims.safe_wording: A mouth care training programme was tested in 14 US nursing homes with 2,152 residents. Over two years it did not show a clear fall in pneumonia: 0.67 cases per 1,000 days residents spent in the homes, against 0.72 without the programme. A later look at the first year alone found fewer pneumonias, but that analysis was not planned in advance, and in the second year pneumonia was slightly (not significantly) more common in the programme homes.
claims.qualifications: Say 'did not show a clear fall', not 'had no effect'. Give the post hoc first-year signal with its status (not planned). The authors link the fade in year two to difficulty keeping the programme going, which supports 'sustaining mouth care is hard', not 'mouth care does not work'. Homes were chosen for high pneumonia rehospitalisation rates.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Post hoc first-year reduction (IRR 0.69) and earlier Japanese trials (Yoneyama 2002) point the other way. The trial tested a staff training programme in routine conditions, not the effect of a clean mouth itself.

claims.claim: A 2022 Cochrane review (6 RCTs, 6244 participants, all high risk of bias) found insufficient evidence of a difference between professional and usual oral care in pneumonia incidence, with low-certainty evidence of fewer pneumonia deaths at 24 months from two small trials.
claims.supporting_passage: "We included six RCTs (6244 participants), all of which were at high risk of bias. Three studies were carried out in Japan, two in the USA, and one in France. The studies evaluated one comparison: professional oral care versus usual oral care." ... "Consistent results from five studies, with 5018 participants, provided insufficient evidence of a difference between professional oral care and usual (simple, self-administered) oral care in the incidence of pneumonia." ... "There was low-certainty evidence from meta-analysis of two individually randomised studies that professional oral care may reduce the risk of pneumonia-associated mortality compared with usual oral care at 24 months' follow-up (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.76, 454 participants). Another study (2513 participants) reported insufficient evidence of a difference for this outcome at 18 months' follow-up. Three studies measured all-cause mortality and identified insufficient evidence of a difference between professional and usual oral care at 12 to 30 months' follow-up." ... "the effect of professional oral care on preventing NHAP remains largely unclear." Full-text excerpt (Scite): "24-month follow-up (Adachi 2002;Yoneyama 2002)."
claims.location: Abstract: Main results; Authors' conclusions. Full text (Scite excerpt): follow-up durations
claims.pico_timeframe: P: nursing home and long-term care residents; I: professional oral care (brushing, swabbing, denture cleaning, mouthrinse or combinations); C: usual (simple, self-administered) oral care; O: pneumonia incidence, pneumonia-associated and all-cause mortality; T: 12 to 30 months
claims.safe_wording: A 2022 Cochrane review pooled six trials in nursing homes, all with a high risk of bias. It concluded that the effect of professional mouth care on preventing pneumonia 'remains largely unclear'. Two small Japanese trials suggested fewer deaths from pneumonia at two years, but the reviewers rated this evidence as low certainty, and a larger study found no clear difference at 18 months.
claims.qualifications: Include the low-certainty signal on pneumonia deaths (judge's instruction) so the post reads as uncertain, not as evidence of no benefit. The comparison is professional vs usual oral care, not mouth care vs none. For the public, do not give the RR; say 'fewer deaths from pneumonia, low-certainty evidence'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Full-text excerpt via Scite gives RR 0.41 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.72; 507 participants) for the same outcome, differing from the abstract (RR 0.43; 454 participants); use the abstract. All-cause mortality showed no clear difference.

"Nurses or caregivers cleaned the patients' teeth by toothbrush after each meal. Swabbing with povidone iodine was additionally used in some cases. Dentists or dental hygienists provided professional care once a week." "During follow-up, pneumonia, febrile days, and death from pneumonia decreased significantly in patients with oral care." claims.supporting_passage: Jablonski 2018 (Introduction): "Mouth care is oral infection control.Inadequate mouth care results in bacterial plaque biofilm accumulation on both teeth and dentures." ... "In addition to serving as the primary etiologic factor for dental caries (tooth decay) and periodontal diseases,increased plaque retention is associated with increased rates of nosocomial pneumonia". claims.safe_wording: Cleaning the mouth removes plaque, the main cause of tooth decay and gum disease. Comfort, being able to eat, and noticing sore spots or broken teeth early are further reasons we should keep doing it, whatever the trials show about pneumonia.
claims.qualifications: Plaque as main cause of decay and gum disease is established background (introduction of Jablonski 2018), not a new finding. 'Comfort, eating, finding sore spots and dignity' as reasons is a clinical and ethical judgement; mark it with 'we should', not as a trial result.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: In 524 community-living people aged 85 and over (453 denture wearers), about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept in their dentures; overnight wearing was independently associated with a higher risk of hospitalisation for or death from pneumonia over 3 years.
claims.supporting_passage: "At baseline, 524 randomly selected seniors (228 men and 296 women; mean age, 87.8 years) were examined for oral health status and oral hygiene behaviors as well as medical assessment, including blood chemistry analysis, and followed up annually until first hospitalization for or death from pneumonia. During a 3-year follow-up period, 48 events associated with pneumonia (20 deaths and 28 acute hospitalizations) were identified. Among 453 denture wearers, 186 (40.8%) who wore their dentures during sleep were at higher risk for pneumonia than those who removed their dentures at night (log rank P = 0.021). In a multivariate Cox model, both perceived swallowing difficulties and overnight denture wearing were independently associated with an approximately 2.3-fold higher risk of the incidence of pneumonia (for perceived swallowing difficulties, hazard ratio [HR], 2.31; and 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11-4.82; and for denture wearing during sleep, HR, 2.38; and 95% CI, 1.25-4.56)"
claims.location: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 524 randomly selected community-living people aged 85+ in Japan (453 denture wearers); E: wearing dentures during sleep (self-reported); C: removing dentures at night; O: first hospitalisation for or death from pneumonia; T: 3 years; multivariable Cox model
claims.safe_wording: In a Japanese study of 524 people aged 85 and over living at home, about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept with their dentures in. Over three years, they were more likely to be admitted to hospital with pneumonia, or to die of it, than those who took their dentures out, even after the researchers allowed for other health differences they measured. This link does not prove that sleeping in dentures causes pneumonia.
claims.qualifications: Observational: say 'linked with', not 'doubles' or 'causes' (the paper's title overstates). People who sleep in dentures may differ in health, frailty or care in ways not measured. Only 48 pneumonia events, so the size of the link is uncertain (hazard ratio 2.38, 95% CI 1.25 to 4.56); do not state an absolute risk (not available in the abstract). Outcome was pneumonia serious enough for admission or death, not all pneumonia. Location: the abstract does not name the city; say 'in Japan'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Lim 2024 meta-analysis (6 non-randomised studies) found no conclusive evidence that wearing removable dentures at all is a risk factor for pneumonia; it did not isolate overnight wear. No trial has tested overnight removal against pneumonia.

claims.safe_wording: Dental specialists advise taking dentures out at night, every night, and cleaning them every day, mainly to prevent sore, inflamed gums under the denture. Follow your own dentist's advice if it differs.
claims.qualifications: Source is an expert review in the American College of Prosthodontists' journal, not UK official guidance (NHS pages could not be opened). The reason given is denture stomatitis; do not present night removal as proven to prevent pneumonia.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Storage method is debated (dry vs cleanser vs water); not needed for the post. The candidate's visual line 'stored as your dentist advises' avoids the dispute.

claims.claim: Dentures are lost in hospital, and labelling them before admission helps.
claims.supporting_passage: Mann 2017: "Eleven out of 12 trusts returned data about how many dentures were lost in their hospitals, between them 695 dentures were reported lost over five years (2011-16)." Doshi 2022 (Abstract): "In total, 123 dentures were reported as lost or broken between 2016-2021. The most commonly reported reasons for loss were patient transfers between wards, being left on hospital trays, or when patients were sleeping. Patients or carers are more likely to report a lost denture compared to hospital staff." ... "Denture loss is a significant financial burden to the NHS, in addition to causing patients and families distress and is most likely under-reported in many hospitals." Doshi 2022 (full text, Scite excerpt): "Labelling dentures is often promoted as an intervention to reduce denture loss, but these findings suggest that this would not help in hospitals where dentures go missing but are not often found." Raveendran 2025: "The use of dentures was recorded in the notes in 46% (11/24) in ward A, 30% (7/23) in ward B and 35% (7/20) in ward C."
claims.location: Mann 2017 Abstract Results; Doshi 2022 Abstract and Discussion (full-text excerpt); Raveendran 2025 Abstract Results
claims.pico_timeframe: UK NHS hospitals: 11 trusts in Kent, Surrey and Sussex 2011 to 2016 (reported losses); one acute hospital 2016 to 2021; three wards at one hospital (67 inpatients), 2025
claims.safe_wording: Dentures do go missing in hospital. Eleven NHS trusts in south-east England reported 695 lost over five years, and hospital dentists think many losses are never reported. In one hospital the commonest moments were moves between wards, dentures left on meal trays, and during sleep. If you or your relative wears dentures, tell the ward staff, keep them in a denture pot, and make sure they are not left on a tray.
claims.qualifications: Loss in hospital is supported. The labelling tip is not: the hospital dentists who studied this say labelling may help less in hospitals, where lost dentures are often not found. Drop 'mark them before a hospital stay' as the main tip, or say labelling helps identify dentures that are found. 'Tell the ward staff' rests on one small service evaluation in which denture use was recorded in the notes for only 30 to 46 in 100 denture wearers across three wards. Figures are reported losses only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Archer 2024 (PMID 38212530, abstract seen in search) suggests labelling is uncommon in care homes, where labelling may help more; not used as a source.

numbers.meaning: dentures reported lost in 11 NHS trusts in Kent, Surrey and Sussex over five years (2011 to 2016); reported losses only

claims.claim: In a randomised trial of 101 nursing home residents with dementia who resisted mouth care, the MOUTh approach doubled the odds of accepting and completing mouth care and lengthened mouth care, but did not clearly reduce resistance or improve oral health.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "One hundred and one nursing home residents with dementia were randomised at the individual level to experimental (n = 55) or control groups (n = 46). One hundred participants provided data for the analyses." "Compared to the control group, persons in the experimental group had twice the odds of allowing mouth care and completing oral hygiene activities; they also allowed longer duration of mouth care (d = 0.56), but showed only small reductions in the intensity of CRBs (d = 0.16) and small differential improvements in oral health (d = 0.18)." Full text, Results 3.1: "During that period, when available for mouth care, NH residents in the experimental group had twice the odds of assenting to mouth care compared to residents in the control group (). Participants in the experimental group had also twice the odds of completing mouth care." Results 3.3: "During the intervention weeks, occurrence of CRB increased in both groups at similar levels (d = 0.01, p = 0.8837)." ... "the magnitude of the effect was small (d=-0.16) and not statistically significant." Methods: "Starting on day 8, participants received mouth care twice daily for three weeks from the trained research assistants." Discussion: "However, the use of research staff to perform the intervention, while supporting internal validity, compromised external validity." "This study also excluded persons with dysphagia."
claims.location: Abstract; full text Methods 2.2, Results 3.1 to 3.4, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 101 residents with moderate to severe dementia who resisted mouth care, 9 US nursing homes; I: MOUTh (threat-reduction techniques plus best-practice mouth care) by trained research assistants; C: best-practice mouth care by research assistants without threat-reduction training; O: primary, occurrence and intensity of care-resistant behaviour and oral health score; secondary, assent, completion and duration of mouth care, analysed per mouth care episode; T: 3-week intervention after 1-week baseline
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial in nine nursing homes, 101 people with dementia who often refused mouth care were split at random into two groups. When carers used a set of calm, step-by-step techniques, mouth care was accepted and finished more often, and lasted longer, than with carers who cleaned teeth well but without those techniques. Refusals did not stop, and over three weeks the trial did not show a clear difference in mouth health.
claims.qualifications: Say 'more often' or (practitioners) 'twice the odds'; never 'twice as likely' (the authors' own discussion uses that phrase, but the analysis gives odds). Results are per mouth care session, so 'more residents accepted' is not accurate; use 'mouth care was accepted more often'. Primary outcomes were not met; the positive findings are secondary. Care was given by trained research staff, not the homes' own staff; people with swallowing difficulty were excluded; three weeks only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Real-world effect when delivered by care home staff is untested in this trial (authors planned a staff implementation study). Assent and completion percentages by group are in tables not returned by the tool.

numbers.meaning: residents randomised (55 experimental, 46 control); 100 analysed
US nursing homes
odds of assenting to, and of completing, mouth care per session, experimental vs control; relative; not 'twice as likely'
extra average increase in mouth care duration in the experimental group (baseline about 2.6 minutes)
small, non-significant differences in resistance intensity and oral health score
intervention period after a 1-week observation period

claims.claim: MOUTh techniques include approaching at eye level, working at a sink and mirror, avoiding elderspeak, cueing with gestures and short commands, bridging (the person holds a toothbrush), chaining (start the task and let the person finish), distraction, hand-over-hand guidance and 'rescue' by a second carer.
claims.supporting_passage: Jablonski 2018 full text, Methods 2.3: "These strategies included: establishing rapport by approaching the resident at or below eye level with a pleasant and calm demeanor; providing mouth care in front of a sink and in front of a mirror (to access procedural or implicit memories); avoiding elderspeak, a type of sing-song “baby talk”; chaining, which involved starting the mouth care and having the older adult finish the task; cueing by using gestures, pantomimes, and short, 1-step commands; distraction; bridging, where the older adult was asked to hold a toothbrush during mouth care; rescue, where a second experimental mouth care provider replaced the first experimental mouth care provider if care-resistant behaviors were escalating; and hand-over-hand, which involved either the older adult placing his or hand over that of the experimental mouth care provider, or the experimental mouth care provider gently guiding the older adult’s hands.The experimental mouth care providers were expected to select strategies on a trial and error basis." Jablonski 2011: "Nurses can safely and effectively provide mouth care to persons with dementia who resist care by using personalized combinations of 15 threat reduction strategies."
claims.location: Jablonski 2018 full text, Methods 2.3 Intervention description; Jablonski 2011 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Description of the intervention as delivered in the trial
claims.safe_wording: The techniques included: coming to the person at or below eye level, calmly; doing mouth care at a sink in front of a mirror; giving the person a toothbrush to hold; starting the brushing and letting them carry on; using gestures and short, one-step instructions; gently guiding their hand; and, if things escalate, letting a different carer take over. Carers tried different techniques to find what worked for each person.
claims.qualifications: The trial tested the package, not each technique separately; do not claim any single technique is proven. Using these in a comic is fine if labelled illustrative.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

numbers.meaning: threat-reduction strategies described in the 2011 practice paper (the 2018 trial lists nine named strategies)

claims.claim: The trial authors concluded that managing refusal may be more realistic than eliminating it.
claims.supporting_passage: "The data suggest that this intervention facilitates mouth care among persons with dementia. The management of refusal behaviour may be a clinically more realistic approach than reducing or eradicating refusals."
claims.location: Abstract: Conclusion
claims.pico_timeframe: As C13-26-a
claims.safe_wording: The researchers concluded that the aim is to get mouth care done despite some refusal, not to make refusal disappear.
claims.qualifications: Authors' interpretation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Resisting mouth care is often a response to feeling threatened.
claims.supporting_passage: "Care-resistant behavior is a fear-evoked response to nurses' unintentionally threatening behavior during mouth care."
claims.location: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Theoretical framework (threat perception), not a measured finding
claims.safe_wording: The approach is built on the idea that pushing a toothbrush away is often fear: having someone put something in your mouth can feel like a threat if you are unable to follow what is happening.
claims.qualifications: This is the authors' theoretical basis, not a trial result; present it as the idea behind the approach. Word it so no carer is blamed (values concern: the source's 'unintentionally threatening behavior' should not become criticism of care workers).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None tested directly.

claims.claim: NICE guidance on care of dying adults (NG31) advises supporting people to drink if they wish and are able, offering frequent mouth and lip care, encouraging family to help if they wish, and assessing and discussing clinically assisted hydration person by person.
claims.supporting_passage: "Support the dying person to drink if they wish to and are able to. Check for any difficulties, such as swallowing problems or risk of aspiration. Discuss the risks and benefits of continuing to drink with the dying person and those involved in the dying person's care." "Encourage people important to the dying person to help with mouth and lip care or giving drinks, if they wish to. Provide any necessary aids and give them advice on giving drinks safely." "Assess, preferably daily, the dying person's hydration status, and review the possible need for starting or continuing clinically assisted hydration, respecting the person's wishes and preferences." "Offer frequent care of the mouth and lips to the dying person, and include the management of dry mouth in their care plan, if needed." "Consider a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration if the person has or is at risk of distressing symptoms or signs that could be associated with dehydration, such as thirst or delirium, and if oral hydration is inadequate." "...review the risks and benefits of continuing clinically assisted hydration with the person and those important to them continue if there are signs of clinical benefit and reduce or stop if there are signs of possible harm to the dying person, such as fluid overload, or if they no longer want it." "The evidence for clinically assisted hydration varied from moderate to very low quality."
claims.location: Clin Med 2016 concise guideline, Box 1 Recommendations (Maintaining hydration) and commentary; full-text excerpts via Scite
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in the last days of life, UK, all settings; guideline published 2015
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance from NICE on the last days of life says: help the person drink if they want to and can; offer frequent care of the mouth and lips; and encourage family to help with mouth care or drinks if they wish, with advice on doing it safely. It says fluids by drip or under the skin should be considered and reviewed for each person, for example if they have distressing thirst and are unable to drink enough, and stopped if they cause harm or the person no longer wants them.
claims.qualifications: NG31 dates from 2015; whether it has been updated could not be checked (NICE site not reachable). The guidance does not say assisted hydration is never appropriate; the post must keep the 'therapeutic trial' option. Mention that 'delirium' appears in the recommendation only if quoting; delirium is not the post's topic.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: NICE rates the evidence on clinically assisted hydration as moderate to very low quality.

numbers.meaning: NICE: monitor people on clinically assisted hydration at least this often for benefit or harm (practitioner detail)

claims.claim: In 32 terminally ill patients in a comfort care unit, most had no hunger or thirst or only at first, and in all patients hunger, thirst and dry mouth could be relieved, usually with small amounts of food and fluid, ice chips and lip lubrication, using far less fluid than needed to prevent dehydration.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ten-bed comfort care unit in a 471-bed long-term care facility." "Mentally aware, competent patients with terminal illnesses monitored from time of admission to time of death while residing in the comfort care unit." "Of the 32 patients monitored during the 12 months of study, 20 patients (63%) never experienced any hunger, while 11 patients (34%) had symptoms only initially. Similarly, 20 patients (62%) experienced either no thirst or thirst only initially during their terminal illness. In all patients, symptoms of hunger, thirst, and dry mouth could be alleviated, usually with small amounts of food, fluids, and/or by the application of ice chips and lubrication to the lips." "In this series, patients terminally ill with cancer generally did not experience hunger and those who did needed only small amounts of food for alleviation. Complaints of thirst and dry mouth were relieved with mouth care and sips of liquids far less than that needed to prevent dehydration."
claims.location: Abstract: Setting, Patients, Results, Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 32 mentally aware, competent terminally ill patients (described as terminally ill with cancer) in a US comfort care unit; no comparator; O: hunger, thirst, dry mouth and what relieved them; T: admission to death, 12-month study, early 1990s
claims.safe_wording: In a small US study of 32 people dying in a comfort care unit, described by the authors as terminally ill with cancer, thirst and a dry mouth were relieved in every case, usually by mouth care, ice chips, moistening the lips and sips of drink. The amounts were far smaller than would be needed to prevent dehydration.
claims.qualifications: Small (32), old (1994), single unit, no comparison group, people able to report symptoms, almost all on opioids. Say it is one small study; do not generalise to all dying older people. 'Usually' belongs to the relief method, not to 'in every case'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No direct comparison with assisted hydration in this study. Evidence in people dying with dementia or frailty is lacking (see C13-11-d).

claims.claim: In a hospice RCT of 129 people with advanced cancer, 1 litre a day of parenteral fluid did not improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life or survival compared with 100 mL.
claims.supporting_passage: "We randomly assigned 129 patients with cancer from six hospices to receive parenteral hydration (normal saline 1 L per day) or placebo (normal saline 100 mL per day) daily over 4 hours. The primary outcome was change in the sum of four dehydration symptoms (fatigue, myoclonus, sedation and hallucinations, 0 = best and 40 = worst possible) between day 4 and baseline." ... "We found no significant differences between the two groups for change in the sum of four dehydration symptoms (-3.3 v -2.8, P = .77)" ... "Overall survival did not differ between the two groups (median, 21 v 15 days, P = .83)." "Hydration at 1 L per day did not improve symptoms, quality of life, or survival compared with placebo."
claims.location: Abstract: Patients and Methods; Results; Conclusion
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 129 adults with advanced cancer in 6 US hospices; I: 1 L/day saline over 4 hours; C: 100 mL/day; O: fatigue, myoclonus, sedation, hallucinations (primary), symptom scales, quality of life, survival; T: day 4 and day 7
claims.safe_wording: In a trial in six US hospices, 129 people with advanced cancer were given either a litre of fluid a day under the skin or into a vein, or a token 100 mL. The larger amount did not show a clear improvement in symptoms, quality of life or survival.
claims.qualifications: Cancer only. Many were not in their last days (median survival 15 to 21 days). The trial's 'dehydration symptoms' were fatigue, twitching, drowsiness and hallucinations, not thirst or dry mouth, so it does not show that drips fail to relieve thirst. Say 'did not show a clear improvement', not 'no effect'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The 2023 Cochrane review found one other trial (200 participants) suggesting longer survival with hydration vs standard care, at very low certainty (C13-11-d).

claims.claim: Evidence on clinically assisted hydration near death comes almost entirely from people with cancer and is very low certainty; it does not transfer to dementia or other non-cancer conditions.
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified one new study (200 participants), for a total of four studies included in this update (422 participants). All participants had a diagnosis of advanced cancer." ... "We are uncertain whether MAH improves survival (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.59; 1 study, 200 participants, very low-certainty evidence)." ... "In adults receiving palliative care in the end stage of their illness, there remains insufficient evidence to determine whether MAH improves QoL or prolongs survival, compared with placebo or standard care. Given that all participants were inpatients with advanced cancer at end of life, our findings are not transferable to adults receiving palliative care in other settings, for non-cancer, dementia or neurodegenerative diseases, or for those with an extended prognosis. Clinicians will need to make decisions based on the perceived benefits and harms of MAH for each individual's circumstances, without the benefit of high-quality evidence to guide them."
claims.location: Abstract: Main results; Authors' conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: P: adults receiving palliative care, all with advanced cancer (4 RCTs, 422 participants); I: medically assisted hydration; C: placebo or standard care; O: quality of life, survival, adverse events; T: days to weeks
claims.safe_wording: The trials on drips near the end of life were all in people with cancer, and a 2023 Cochrane review found too little evidence to say whether they improve comfort or prolong life. The reviewers say the results do not apply to people dying with dementia or other conditions, so the decision has to be made for each person.
claims.qualifications: An evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit. Keep the post from implying drips are never right.

claims.claim: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies in people aged 60 and over, bladder (urological) medicines, antidepressants and psycholeptics were associated with dry mouth in intervention studies, and the number of medicines was associated with dry mouth in observational studies; risk was greatest for drugs for urinary incontinence.
claims.supporting_passage: "Older people (aged ≥60) who participated in intervention or observational studies investigating drug use as an exposure and xerostomia or salivary gland hypofunction as adverse drug outcomes." ... "Of 1,544 potentially relevant studies, 52 were deemed eligible for inclusion in the final review and 26 in metaanalyses. The majority of studies were of moderate methodological quality. In the intervention studies, urological medications (odds ratio (OR) = 5.91, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 4.04-8.63; I = 62%), antidepressants (OR = 4.74, 95% CI = 2.69-8.32, I = 21%), and psycholeptics (OR = 2.59, 95% CI = 1.79-3.95, I = 0%) were significantly associated with dry mouth. In the observational studies, numbers of medications and several medication classes were significantly associated with xerostomia and salivary gland hypofunction." "Medication use was significantly associated with xerostomia and salivary gland hypofunction in older adults. The risk of dry mouth was greatest for drugs used for urinary incontinence."
claims.location: Abstract: Participants; Results; Conclusion
claims.pico_timeframe: P: people aged 60+; E: specific drug classes or number of medicines; C: placebo/comparator (intervention studies) or non-users (observational); O: xerostomia or reduced saliva flow; literature 1990 to 2016
claims.safe_wording: A review of 52 studies in people aged 60 and over found dry mouth was linked with several kinds of medicine. The link was strongest for bladder medicines taken for leaking urine, and antidepressants were also linked. The more medicines people took, the more often they had a dry mouth.
claims.qualifications: Use 'linked with' (the review reports associations, per the editor's guidance). No absolute rates are available: do not give numbers to the public, and never turn the odds ratios into 'X times more likely'. Name at most one or two drug types in plain words; 'psycholeptics' is a WHO drug-classification group, and any plain gloss of it comes from that classification, not from the abstract.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneity for urological drugs (I2 62%); most studies moderate quality.

numbers.meaning: included in review
odds of dry mouth with urological drugs, antidepressants, psycholeptics vs comparison in intervention studies; relative; practitioners only

claims.claim: Saliva protects teeth, and a dry mouth increases the risk of tooth decay; it also makes chewing, swallowing, taste and denture wearing harder.
claims.supporting_passage: Plemons 2014: "Chronic xerostomia significantly increases the risk of experiencing dental caries, demineralization, tooth sensitivity, candidiasis and other oral diseases that may affect quality of life negatively." Müller 2023 (Abstract): "These conditions negatively affect oral functions, such as chewing, swallowing, speech, and taste. Additionally, the lack of lubrication of the oral mucosa frequently leads to super-infections with candida. Denture retention and comfort may also be compromised. The risk of dental caries and erosion of natural teeth increases since saliva, which is essential for repairing initial lesions in tooth structures, is insufficient." Müller 2023 (Introduction): "Saliva plays a vital role in maintaining the health of hard and soft tissues in the oral cavity. It helps remove food debris, neutralize acids, and protect against bacterial infections, thereby preventing dental caries, periodontal disease, and mucositis"
claims.location: Plemons 2014 Abstract; Müller 2023 Abstract and Introduction (full text)
claims.pico_timeframe: Professional guidance and narrative review; background physiology
claims.safe_wording: Saliva washes the mouth, neutralises acid and helps repair early damage to teeth. When the mouth is dry, tooth decay becomes more likely, and chewing, swallowing, tasting food and keeping dentures in place can all get harder.
claims.qualifications: Dental professional guidance (US) and a narrative review; widely agreed, not a new finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: Sucking sugary sweets to relieve dryness increases decay risk; sugar-free gum or lozenges and sips of water are preferred.
claims.supporting_passage: Müller 2023: "Sucking lozenges should not be too acidic or contain sugar, as the latter increases the risk of caries and tooth loss." "Salivation can also be stimulated by sucking on sweets, although sour drops may cause dental erosion and are therefore less suitable than aromatic lozenges or liquorice. Care should also be taken to ensure that they contain no sugar to prevent the development of tooth decay." "it is unfortunate that all chewing gums presently accessible on the market adhere to denture acrylic, thus rendering the act of chewing exceptionally arduous." "Hence, the derived recommendations listed inandare non-exhaustive and not based on scientific evidence". Plemons 2014: "It also should focus on various palliative and preventive measures, including pharmacological treatment with salivary stimulants, topical fluoride interventions and the use of sugar-free chewing gum to relieve dry-mouth symptoms and improve the patient's quality of life."
claims.location: Müller 2023 full text, sections 9 and 10; Plemons 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Expert recommendations; not trial evidence
claims.safe_wording: Dental advice for a dry mouth is to take frequent sips of water and, if you still have your own teeth, to use sugar-free gum or sugar-free lozenges. Sucking sugary sweets for relief raises the risk of tooth decay.
claims.qualifications: Expert advice, not trial evidence (Müller et al. say their dietary recommendations are not evidence-based). Gum sticks to dentures, so suggest it for people with their own teeth. Saliva sprays: Müller mentions artificial saliva after discussion with a dentist or doctor; keep 'ask which saliva spray or gel suits you'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: An umbrella review (Conte 2025, seen only in Consensus search, not opened) rated most reviews of dry mouth treatments low quality; relief from substitutes is short-lived.

claims.claim: If a medicine may be causing dry mouth, it is reasonable to ask a GP or pharmacist to review it.
claims.supporting_passage: Müller 2023: "The European Society of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) guideline in geriatrics acknowledges this risk [,]. In cases of malnutrition or risk of malnutrition, this guideline provides guidance for nutritional support and recommends strategies such as reducing or replacing medications that contribute to xerostomia." Plemons 2014: "A systematic approach to xerostomia management can facilitate interdisciplinary patient care, including collaboration with physicians regarding systemic conditions and medication use."
claims.location: Müller 2023 full text, section 8; Plemons 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Guidance statements (ESPEN via secondary report; ADA)
claims.safe_wording: If your mouth is often dry, ask your GP or pharmacist whether any of your medicines could be the cause, whether each one is still needed, and whether there is an alternative. Do not stop a medicine on your own.
claims.qualifications: ESPEN recommendation is reported second-hand by Müller 2023 and applies to people with or at risk of malnutrition; the ADA summary recommends collaboration on medication use. 'Do not stop a medicine on your own' is standard safety advice, not from these sources.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial shows that deprescribing relieves dry mouth in older people; not searched further.

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported by abstracts of the two key sources. Zimmerman 2020 (2,152 residents, 14 US nursing homes): no significant fall in pneumonia over 2 years (0.67 vs 0.72 per 1,000 resident-days), a post hoc first-year reduction, and non-significantly more pneumonia in year two. Cao 2022 Cochrane: effect on pneumonia 'remains largely unclear', low-certainty evidence of fewer pneumonia deaths at 24 months from two small Japanese trials, and no trials of mouth care against none. Yoneyama 2002 confirmed as an earlier positive, high-risk-of-bias trial. As the judge asked, the post must carry the post hoc and pneumonia-death signals so it reads as uncertain, not as 'does not work'. The 'firmer reasons' line is judgement plus established dental background and must be marked as such.

Core claim supported as an association: Iinuma 2015 (524 people aged 85+, Japan): about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept in them, and overnight wear was independently linked with hospital admission or death from pneumonia over 3 years (48 events; adjusted HR 2.38, 95% CI 1.25 to 4.56), plus more plaque, gum inflammation and Candida. Night removal advice sourced to an expert review (McReynolds 2023) because the NHS pages could not be opened. The hospital loss claim is supported (695 dentures reported lost in 11 trusts over 5 years; commonest moments: ward moves, meal trays, sleep). The candidate's tip to label dentures before a hospital stay is not supported: the same hospital dentists say labelling may not help in hospital because lost dentures are often not found. Drop 'doubles' and the labelling tip.
candidates.revised_angle: Taking dentures out at night is standard dental advice and was linked with fewer serious pneumonias in a study of people aged 85 and over (an association, not proof). Clean them daily. In hospital, dentures go missing mostly during ward moves, on meal trays and at night: tell the ward staff the person wears dentures, keep them in a denture pot, and check they are not left on a tray. Any mention of labelling should say it helps identify dentures that are found, not that it prevents loss.

candidates.reason: Supported from the trial full text, which also describes the intervention (Methods 2.3), so the named techniques are sourced as the judge required. Jablonski 2018 (101 residents with dementia, 9 US nursing homes, 3 weeks): mouth care was accepted and completed more often (twice the odds per session) and lasted longer. However, resistance was not reduced and mouth health showed no clear difference; these were the primary outcomes. Required wording: 'more often', never 'twice as likely' and not 'more residents accepted' (the analysis is per session). State that trained research staff gave the care, that people with swallowing problems were excluded, and that refusals continued. The fear/threat idea is the authors' theory and must be presented that way, without blaming care workers.

All essential claims supported. NICE NG31 recommendations were read verbatim in the published concise guideline (Clin Med 2016): support drinking if wished, frequent mouth and lip care, family helping if they wish, and case-by-case review of assisted hydration including a therapeutic trial. McCann 1994: thirst and dry mouth relieved in all 32 patients with mouth care and sips (small, old, cancer). Bruera 2013: 1 L/day did not show clear benefit over 100 mL in 129 hospice cancer patients, but its symptoms were not thirst or dry mouth. Buchan 2023 Cochrane: evidence is all in cancer, very low certainty, and not transferable to dementia or non-cancer conditions. The post must name the cancer limitation, keep the drip as a separate decision for each person (not 'never'), and be coordinated with C19 so it runs once.

Reserve; ready if promoted. Tan 2018: bladder medicines, antidepressants and psycholeptics linked with dry mouth in people aged 60+, strongest for incontinence drugs; number of medicines also linked (associations; odds ratios only). The editor's requirement for a dental source is met: ADA Council on Scientific Affairs 2014 (dry mouth raises decay risk; sugar-free gum) and Müller 2023 (saliva protects teeth; lozenges should contain no sugar, though this is expert advice, not trial evidence). Delivering better oral health could not be opened. Use no drug-effect numbers for the public; note that gum sticks to dentures.
